source: Jaynes (1973) The well-posed problem
finding: Jaynes argued Bertrand's chord problem has one answer (1/2) once the problem is required to be invariant to circle size and position. He tested it by tossing broom straws onto a circle.
numbers: 128 successful tosses onto a 5-inch circle, chord lengths grouped in 10 categories; fit to the predicted distribution gave an 'embarrassingly low' chi-squared. Theory answer: P(chord longer than triangle side)=1/2.
quote: 128 successful tosses confirmed Eq. (13) with an embarrassingly low value of chi-squared
limits: Single lab, 128 tosses, author-run. The experiment fixes a toss procedure, so it confirms that procedure, not a unique prior in general.
agent_relevance: A 'maximally uninformative' prior is only defined relative to stated invariances and a stated procedure. The agent should not claim an ignorance prior without naming the reference class and procedure.

source: Drory (2015) Failure and uses of Jaynes' principle of transformation groups
finding: Drory shows the same symmetry arguments Jaynes used also yield Bertrand's other two answers (1/3 and 1/4), depending on how chords are generated. Jaynes' invariance method does not remove the ambiguity of indifference.
numbers: Own experiment: stick released at a random point on a circle edge. 700 attempts, 363 successes (0.518). Of successes, chord longer than inscribed triangle side in 123 cases, proportion 0.339, close to the predicted 1/3 (Jaynes' value is 1/2).
limits: One-person tabletop experiment; the author notes sensitivity to systematic tilt errors. A theory paper, not a population replication.
agent_relevance: Two physical procedures, both respecting the same invariances, give different 'objective' answers. Priors need a stated generating procedure, which is what a class record supplies.

source: Shackel (2007) Bertrand's paradox and the principle of indifference; Marinoff (1994) A resolution of Bertrand's paradox
finding: Search-result summary only: Marinoff (1994) says the problem is vaguely posed and clear variants have different consistent answers (distinction strategy). Shackel says that strategy fails and Jaynes' symmetry requirement does not resolve the paradox.
numbers: No numbers seen.
limits: Not opened; secondhand snippet. Verify before citing.
agent_relevance: Philosophy of science still treats the indifference principle as unresolved. Do not build the agent on it.

source: Zhu and Griffiths (2024) Eliciting the priors of large language models using iterated in-context learning
finding: Iterated learning (a Gibbs sampler where each step's output seeds the next) recovers GPT-4's implicit prior. Elicited priors qualitatively match published human priors for causal strength, proportions and everyday quantities.
numbers: 100 chains of 12 iterations per task. Causal-strength chains reached a stationary distribution by iteration 7 (generative) and 8 (preventive), Mann-Whitney p<.05. Speculative events, median completion year: superhuman AI 2042, zero carbon 2045, Mars colony 2050.
quote: The key assumption of our proposed method is that LLMs behave as Bayesian agents
limits: Match with human priors is by visual comparison only; human raw data not available. Only GPT-4. Assumes the LLM acts as a Bayesian agent, which the authors flag as unproven. Priors over future events cannot be checked.
agent_relevance: A measurable way to read the model's implicit prior without trusting its verbal answer. A class record can be compared against it to flag where the model's prior is off.

source: Zhu and Griffiths (2024) coin-flip proportion task
finding: In the coin-flip proportion task GPT-4's chains drifted toward 0 and 1, the U-shaped prior seen in humans.
numbers: Chains gradually concentrated mass near p=0 or 1 over 12 iterations; GPT-4 prior judged to match human prior in shape.
limits: Qualitative match; a uniform-prior comparison was not formally run for proportions.
agent_relevance: The model's default prior for a bias parameter is not uniform. Do not assume the model starts neutral.

source: Li and Rui (2024) Dual traits in probabilistic reasoning of LLMs: Jason test
finding: With an uncharacteristic description, most LLMs use the base rate correctly. With a stereotypical description they almost ignore it, like humans in the lawyer-engineer problem.
numbers: Posterior-odds ratio between 75% and 25% base-rate conditions (normative 9), uncharacteristic description: gpt-4o 9, gpt-4 9, claude-3-opus 8.86, gemini-1.5-pro 6.36, mistral-large 3, llama-3-70b 9, humans 2.25. Representative CS description: ratios 1.18 to 2.58 (humans 2.02). Humanities: 1.00 to 1.60 (humans 1.99).
limits: Six models, one task family. Human column is reconstructed from published figures, not run in parallel.
agent_relevance: Prior use depends on how vivid the case description is. Our S0 gate should present the class record before the case detail and as a number.

source: Li and Rui (2024) unstructured test: prior versus posterior correlation
finding: When the model must recall base rates itself, its posterior rank order runs against the true prior and tracks similarity to the field.
numbers: Prior vs posterior Spearman -0.84 to -0.90 across five models; posterior vs similarity Spearman 0.87 to 0.94, Pearson up to 0.98. Field B prior was 4 to 10 times field A, yet the model ranked A highest because the description matched A.
limits: Small design (three fields, one description). Correlations are over few items.
agent_relevance: Strong evidence that recall of the prior fails first. This is the case for a measured, injected prior instead of asking the model to remember one.

source: Li and Rui (2024) prompt engineering and recall consistency
finding: Changing one word to force step-by-step Bayes computation reversed the bias in the semi-structured test. In the unstructured test even four increasingly explicit prompts did not fix it, and recalled priors were inconsistent.
numbers: GPT-4o gave a field A prior of 2% to 4% when asked directly but used 10% to 30% in the posterior judgment. Correlations stayed the same size and direction across four prompt revisions.
limits: One model (GPT-4o) examined in detail for the prompt series.
agent_relevance: Self-reported priors are unstable. Use code to compute the posterior from a stored prior rather than asking the model to combine them.

source: Qiu et al. (2026) Bayesian teaching enables probabilistic reasoning in LLMs: baseline
finding: In a 5-round flight-recommendation task, off-the-shelf LLMs fall far short of a Bayesian assistant and mostly stop improving after round one. Chain-of-thought and numeric formats did not help.
numbers: Bayesian Assistant (uniform prior) final-round accuracy 81%; random baseline 37%; off-the-shelf models roughly 36% to 58% after 5 rounds; 624 simulated users, 100 new test flight sets per round. Humans (48 users) improved more than most LLMs but stayed below 81%.
limits: Synthetic users; accuracy is agreement with the user's choice. Models include Gemma 2, Llama 3, Qwen 2.5, GPT-4.1 Mini, Gemini 1.5 Pro. Range read from figure labels.
agent_relevance: A loop that must update on repeated evidence cannot rely on the model's own updating. Counting and updating belong in code.

source: Qiu et al. (2026) Bayesian teaching: fine-tuning result
finding: Fine-tuning on the Bayesian assistant's predictions beats fine-tuning on the user's true choices (oracle teaching) and generalizes to hotel and web-shopping tasks.
numbers: Bayesian-tuned models agree with the Bayesian Assistant about 80% of the time, significantly more than original and oracle-tuned models.
limits: Needs fine-tuning, which our scaffold-only setting excludes. Uniform prior used; other priors performed similarly (appendix).
agent_relevance: Shows the weak step is the update, not world knowledge. Supports a code-side posterior.

source: Qiu et al. (2026) appendix D.1: priors the LLMs bring
finding: Unprimed LLMs recommend flights better than chance before any interaction, so they carry human-like priors. Users whose preferences deviate from the model's prior are harder to learn.
numbers: Gemma 2 9B prior: mostly 'no preference', moderate preference for fewer stops. Gemini 1.5 Pro prior: diffuse, prefers cheaper, shorter, earlier flights. Regression of accuracy on L2 distance from the prior: negative coefficient for original Gemma, much smaller for the Bayesian assistant and Bayesian-tuned Gemma, all p<0.001.
limits: Verbalized priors may not match the prior actually used (authors note). Two models.
agent_relevance: A strong implicit prior costs accuracy on atypical cases. A measured class prior helps most when the case is atypical.

source: Weber, Binder and Krauss (2018) Why can only 24% solve Bayesian reasoning problems in natural frequencies
finding: Even when a problem is given in natural frequencies, many students convert it back to probabilities and then fail. The paper also restates the McDowell and Jacobs (2017) meta-analysis headline numbers.
numbers: N=180 university students (114 first sample, 66 to 69 replication). 49% chose probability calculation although the neutral frame was frequency; natural frequencies were the preferred calculation format for about 34%. Table: correct about 36% with natural frequencies vs 20% with probabilities. Meta-analysis cited: 24% correct in frequency format vs 4% in probability format.
limits: German students taught probability-first; the einstellung explanation is interpretive. The 24% and 4% figures are cited, not recomputed here.
agent_relevance: Format helps a lot but is not enough. Present class records as counts out of a stated sample and let code do the division.

source: McDowell and Jacobs (2017) Meta-analysing the effect of natural frequencies on Bayesian reasoning
finding: Per search summary of the 2016 conference abstract: 30 papers, 90 effects; natural frequency format beats probabilities.
numbers: Headline via Weber et al. (2018): 24% correct with natural frequencies vs 4% with probabilities.
limits: Page did not load. I did not read the abstract itself. Effect-size statistics unverified.
agent_relevance: Format effect is real but modest in absolute terms.

source: Koehler (1996) The base rate fallacy reconsidered
finding: Review of the base-rate literature. Base rates are almost always used to some degree; use rises when rates are learned implicitly, framed as frequencies, reliable, or more diagnostic than the individuating information.
numbers: No numbers on the abstract page I could read; the article body was not available.
quote: base rates are almost always used; degree depends on task structure and representation
limits: Only the abstract was read. Normative claim: few tasks fit the narrow Bayes template, so calling neglect a fallacy is often wrong.
agent_relevance: Boundary conditions for when a prior is used: reliability, frequency format, diagnosticity. These can be logged in a class record.

source: Talboy and Fuller (2023) Challenging the appearance of machine intelligence: cognitive bias in LLMs
finding: Mammography base-rate problem given to ChatGPT 3.5, GPT-4 and Bard. With numbers present, models usually invoked Bayes, but not consistently across retests. With numbers removed, outputs copied the incidence rate or the sensitivity.
numbers: Correct answer: 7.7% positive predictive value. Non-numeric version: both GPT models answered 10% (incidence), Bard 80% (sensitivity). Bard in March gave 10%, in August used Bayes. ChatGPT 3.5 used Bayes in March, not in August.
limits: Small set of single prompts through chat interfaces; retest drift confounds model updates with sampling noise. Not a systematic benchmark.
agent_relevance: Same number-selection error humans make. Retest drift means prior behavior must be measured in the loop, not assumed.

source: Macmillan-Scott and Musolesi (2024) (Ir)rationality and cognitive biases in LLMs
finding: Seven LLMs on 12 classic reasoning tasks (including a base-rate style AIDS task, Linda, Monty Hall, Wason). LLMs err, but mostly not in human-like ways, and answers vary between runs.
numbers: Each task prompted 10 times. GPT-4 correct with correct reasoning 69.2%; Claude 2 55.0%. Llama 2 7B incorrect 77.5%. Human-like bias in GPT-3.5 only 21.7% of cases (50.8% counting human-like correct ones). Llama 2 70B refused 41.7%.
limits: Default parameters, no system prompt, zero-shot. Task familiarity may inflate results for tasks seen in training.
agent_relevance: Do not read LLM errors as human-style bias. Inconsistency across runs is itself a risk; repeat and count.

source: CogBias (2026) Measuring and mitigating cognitive bias in LLMs
finding: Unified benchmark across four bias families. Judgment biases (including base-rate neglect) occur at a moderate rate, and prompt-level debiasing made them worse, not better.
numbers: 5,300 instances; GPT-4o-mini, Llama-3.3-70B, Qwen2.5-72B at T=0. Judgment bias rate 19.8%, shifts of 2.7 to 7.7 points. Prompt debiasing: Judgment accuracy -4.4%; Response biases +40.5% position independence. Linear probes separate biased from neutral at 99.8% for Judgment.
limits: Preprint under review; one representative dataset per family; cross-family magnitudes not comparable.
agent_relevance: Telling the model 'do not neglect base rates' does not reliably work. Structural fixes (code-side prior) are better.

source: Selby et al. (2025) Had enough of experts? Quantitative knowledge retrieval from LLMs: prior elicitation
finding: Elicited parametric priors from LLMs and compared them to human expert priors. Model differences exceeded task differences; Pearson-correlation priors looked unlike the experts'.
numbers: LLM priors for Cohen's d centred on 0.2 to 0.25, GPT-4 around 0.5. Mistral-7B gave t priors with nu=30, Llama-70B nu=5. Llama models gave more conservative priors, GPT more informative; some Mistral priors had effective sample size over 1000.
limits: 2023-vintage open and proprietary models; no gold standard for a 'good prior'. Possible data leakage noted.
agent_relevance: Prior width varies by model and may be overconfident. Use the model prior only as a weak default and cap its weight.

source: Selby et al. (2025) imputation experiment and leakage test
finding: LLM imputation did not consistently beat classical methods. A dataset-recognition test suggests some good LLM scores come from memorised data.
numbers: 64 OpenML-CC18 datasets, 80/20 split. KNN and random forest beat mean imputation consistently; most LLM methods did not. Llama 2 70B beat mean imputation in 4 of 5 domains, Llama 2 13B in 3, Mixtral and Mistral in 2. Recognition of 11 datasets from one row: GPT-3.5 6, Gemini 1.5 Pro 5, Llama 2 70B 2.
limits: Tabular imputation only; not about elicited priors directly.
agent_relevance: Memorised data can pass as prior knowledge. Check priors against a held-out class record.

source: Capstick et al. (2025) AutoElicit: LLMs for expert prior elicitation in predictive modelling
finding: LLM-elicited Gaussian priors for linear models reduce error and need fewer labels than an uninformative prior, and beat using in-context learning alone.
numbers: Synthetic task: an order of magnitude lower test MSE after 5 examples, equal MSE by 20. Heart Disease: GPT-3.5 returned an uninformative prior when unsure (same accuracy as baseline); GPT-4-turbo and DeepSeek-R1-32B gave better ones. UTI dementia task: same peak accuracy at about 15 labels, 220 days earlier; over 6 months of labelling saved.
limits: Small linear models; 10 splits; some tasks show memorisation (hypothyroid). A Bayes factor is needed to choose among priors.
agent_relevance: Prior choice can be validated against data with a Bayes factor. The model defaulting to uninformative when unsure is a behavior worth preserving.

source: Arai et al. (2025) How many patients could we save with LLM priors?
finding: LLM-informed hyperparameter priors for hierarchical adverse-event models beat meta-analytic priors on one real trial, and allowed the same predictive score with less data.
numbers: Trial NCT00617669. Best: Llama 3.3 70B, blind prompt, T=1.0. 80% of training data with LLM priors (LPD -4.093) beat the meta-analytic baseline with 100% (LPD -4.103); about 66 fewer patients (328 to 262). Higher temperature gave more variable priors, more so for MedGemma 27B. Disease-informed prompts did not beat blind prompts.
limits: One disease area, one dataset, two models. The LPD gap is tiny (0.010) and no interval for it appears in the text I read.
agent_relevance: Gain is small and unproven beyond one dataset. Prior variability grows with temperature; sample the prior at low temperature or aggregate.

source: Huang (2025) LLM-BI: fully automated Bayesian inference with LLMs
finding: Proof of concept: an LLM turned plain-language beliefs into priors for Bayesian linear regression, and in a second experiment specified priors and likelihood from a one-sentence task description.
numbers: Experiment II posterior mean recovered 1.823 vs ground truth 1.8 for one parameter; Experiment I posteriors nearly identical to a manually specified model.
limits: Two toy experiments, one model, no repeats. A web summary said repeated calls gave different priors (not confirmed in the text I read).
agent_relevance: Weak evidence. Treat as a feasibility demo only.

source: Xie et al. (2022) An explanation of in-context learning as implicit Bayesian inference
finding: Theory plus synthetic GINC dataset: in-context learning works because pretraining data is a mixture over latent concepts with a prior; the prompt picks the concept by Bayesian inference.
numbers: In-context accuracy rises with number of examples and example length. Single-concept pretraining gives flat curves; random-transition data fails; unseen concepts fail. 12 vs 16 layers at equal validation loss 1.33: accuracy 81% to 85%. Example order changes accuracy by 10 to 40 points for the same example set.
limits: Synthetic HMM data, small models; assumes distinguishability. Relation to real LLMs is an analogy.
agent_relevance: The prior in a pretrained model is the mix of concepts in its data, not a chosen ignorance prior. Order effects mean the loop should shuffle and repeat.

source: Arora et al. (2025) Bayesian scaling laws for in-context learning
finding: A Bayesian law for in-context learning has an explicit task prior. Fitting it shows post-training mostly shifts the prior over tasks, not task knowledge.
numbers: On synthetic SFT, the Bayesian law was behind but competitive with baselines (logistic law lowest NRMSE). The prior shifts suddenly toward the favoured HMM as SFT data grows, and shifts more slowly in larger models. For Llama 3.1 8B Instruct, the prior on unsafe behaviors fell but many-shot jailbreaking still saturated the posterior.
limits: GPT-2 sized models for most experiments; real-model results are on one model pair.
agent_relevance: Priors can be reweighted by tuning but evidence can overwhelm them. A scaffold's injected prior should be strong enough to matter against in-context noise.

source: Halawi et al. (2024) Approaching human-level forecasting with language models
finding: Retrieval, fine-tuning and ensembling bring a LM forecaster near the human crowd. Base LMs without these are poor; prompts ask for historical base rates.
numbers: Test set from after June 2023. Random baseline Brier 0.250; human crowd 0.149; best base model (GPT-4-1106) 0.208; final system 0.179, accuracy 71.5% vs crowd 77.0%. RMS calibration error 0.42 vs crowd 0.38. System is best when the crowd is less confident and when it retrieves many articles.
limits: Binary questions from 5 platforms. Still worse than the crowd overall. The base-rate instruction is not isolated as a cause.
agent_relevance: A forecasting prior is mainly a reference class. Retrieval of the class history gives the largest gain. This matches the S0 class-record gate.

source: Kadavath et al. (2022) Language models (mostly) know what they know
finding: Large models are well calibrated on multiple-choice and true/false questions in the right format. P(IK) probes work in-distribution and partly transfer, but calibration breaks on new task types.
numbers: Calibration improves with model size and few-shot prompts. RLHF models are miscalibrated but a temperature adjustment restores fair calibration. P(IK) is poorly calibrated out of distribution.
limits: Anthropic models of 2022; format-sensitive; a 'None of the above' option harms calibration. No single headline number extracted.
agent_relevance: Model confidence can be a weak input but must be recalibrated against our own records before use as a prior.

source: Tversky and Kahneman 1974; Bar-Hillel 1980; Barbey and Sloman 2007 (base-rate respect)
finding: Cited by the opened LLM papers as the human reference results: people lean on representativeness and often ignore base rates, with frequency formats and causal framing restoring use. I did not open these papers.
numbers: None recorded (not opened).
limits: Secondhand through the opened LLM papers.
agent_relevance: Human data is the comparison point for LLM tests; verify exact numbers before use.
